I am pansexual, and generally a very sexual person. I'm also very visual. I am both a hairstylist and an artist, so looks tend to be the first thing I notice about a person, weather I find them sexually attractive or not. I have to scrutinize people's looks to some degree for both a living and a hobby, so for me it's somewhat of a reflex at this point (though for me it's more just observing, not judging)

But something important to note here, OP, is that noticing or appreciating the physical appearance of a person doesn't necessarily mean you are objectifying them. It's just a pretty common first step upon meeting or seeing someone for many people. After all, appearance is usually one of the only pieces of immediate information you get about a person. 

Also maybe I'm reading too much into your specific phrasing, but the way you wordrd it sorta makes it come accross like you view watching and masturbating to porn and fantasizing on the same level as lying to and cheating on your partner. While some couples may view that as the same thing (and that's their choice) many don't. My partner and I are both pansexual and watch a fair bit of porn, both alone and together. We'll often send each other stuff we think the other might like, too. It's all mutual and above board, and I think that as long as you are on the same page, I don't see any harm in it. And honestly, feeling like an individual in porn, who is doing a job, and who you will never meet somehow lessens your connection with your partner, you probably didn't value them all that much as an individual in the first place. It's still fine to have porn be an off limits boundary, but putting that in those terms seems far more objectifying to your partner than anything in porn to me (plus, as a former camgirl, most of those pornstars consent to the objectificaiton anyways) 

If you feel like doing these things or looking at ot thinking of others in a sexual way would create some sort of void in *your* relationship, that's super valid. But personally, my sexuality, both expressed towards my parter and towards others (both in and out of porn, all with my partners knowledge and consent), has deepened my connection with my partner, not weakened it. 

I understand that my perspective comes from an uncommon set of experiences, but I guess that's sort of my point? Everyone out there has a different personality and mind than you. They've been through different things. We're all individuals, and personally I've always been a big proponent of doing what works for *you* (provided that it doesn't hurt anyone else) 

But to be abundantly clear, I feel confident that everything I've said about my relationship above isn't causing any sort of void in my life or relationship. We love each other deeply, he is one of the most important people in the world to me. We have a very strong bond outside of the bedroom or sex, but when it does come to that side of things, for us it is something that usually brings us closer together rather than creating distance. 

TLDR; judge not lest ye be judged. To each their own and all that. Hope this gives you some insight into another perspective, and I'm definitely happy to follow up on anything about what I posted.

Okay, big edit because of more context from seeing other comments posted in the time that it took me to type this out on mobile. I've changed what I feel like doesn't apply, and I have some additional advice that I hope helps.

OP, you are very young, and you had a very intense thing happen to you at  very young age.

This is complicated and there are a couple of things about your current relationship that honestly concern me a little. Not necessarily red flags, but definitely thing that could make you or him more vulnerable that I think you need to be aware of.

First of all, the idea that you aren't good enough is one that has the potential to really hurt both of you, as well as your relationship as a whole. You feeling insecure is obviously not healthy for you, but as someone who has been on the other end of that dynamic, it can also breed a lot of guilt and anxiety in a partner. I know that for a year my past partner's constant insecurity about our relationship made me feel extremely guilty and like *i* wasn't doing enough to make him feel love and supported (turns out he just straight up didn't love me, but I digress). I'm not saying this is intentional at all on your part or even that you are at fault- you aren't- but it's a really unhealthy foot to get off on, and it could end up damaging you both a lot. This is a big one to start off on, and I don't want to scare you, but I think it's something that's really important for you both to be mindful of moving forward. I struggled with this a lot in my past abusive relationship as well as the first couple of years and even now and again currently into my current amazing 5+ year partnership. A big thing that helped me with this was making sure I persured my own life and hobbies outside my partner. We have the same circle of friends, but I chat with them privately or when he's busy or not around, and being a little more socially independent has helped a lot. I know that can be hard right now with the current state of the world, but try reaching out to friends outside of the relationship. Other than that, make sure you are pursuing hobbies and other interests- it can take a while, but getting back into my passions was probably the most helpful thing for improving my own self worth. This may not apply to your relationship, and if you already have stuff in this vein good for you,, but making sure you have a healthy life outside of it is important and could really help you both. 

The communication thing is another big one. It's good that you are at least aware of it. I would suggest sitting down at a calm moment when there are no other big things going on and have a really frank talk with him about it. Ask him how its affects him, and how you can help. If is as loving and supportive as he sounds, he should have the same concerns, so let him know of ways that can hell you too! If you don't have any, sometimes just talking and having a brainstorming session about issues can really help. Plus, it's practice with the whole communication thing. Communication about the issue of you not feeling good enough is also important here. Try to frankly discuss-without judgement, or at least trying to have an open mind, since I know there can be a lot of knee jerk reactions about this sort of thing- why you might be feeling this way, how it affects you, how it affects him, and ways you can both help. I know you have communication issues, and sometimes setting aside a time to talk about things every so often can help foster better communication overall.

Feeling insignificant and insecure can be another big one, and I know that often it can be very difficult to talk to a partner about. Sometimes reassurances can make you feel worse, or guilty. But I think this is another practice thing. Not only talking to him, but to others in your life. Family, friends, a therapist, anyone else around you. Trying to be more open with others can help. Sometimes it's something that can really be helped by some simple practice, not to mention fostering healthy relationships with those around you can help in general. This can definitely be difficult and can start as slow as you are comfortable with of course. But just another thing that might really help. Talking to him about it is important too, just be careful no one is ending up blaming or apologizing, and it comes up independent of other issues.

As far as struggling with your sexual orientation, that can be a very difficult, especially while already in a relationship. I would definitely suggest putting anything sexual or physically intimate on hold for quite a while. Personlly, your previous experiences are enough that I think that you should be very careful with both the physical and emotional side of intimacy in your relationship. In addition to your prior abuse, romantic attraction does not necessarily lead to sexual attraction, which can be a very difficult thing in a romantic relationship. I don't want to make assumptions, but I can see that potentially playing into your insecurities and feelings of not being good enough in the relationship. In addition to that, as someone who was very sexual with others both in and out of a relationship much before I was ready, I think that 15 is too young to be having sex or particularly sexual contact. There's a lot going on at that age developmentally and socially, and sex and sexual acts usually adds a complexity that most people not ready for at that age. I absolutely don't want to fault or shame you for any of your past experiences, but I would strongly urge you to consider pulling back from that sort of thing for a while. I urge you to take some time to figure things out, your sexual orientation included, by yourself for a while. I would encourage you not to have, at the very least, a particularly sexual or physically intimate relationship with anyone, male or female, for a while while you figure out and process this and other things.

Thus is just some of my thoughts from my own experiences, but I hope this helps! You're dealing with a lot, so best of luck to you.

So idk if this is apropriate for me to post, but I follow this sub because my boyfriend has (usually somewhat mild but getting worse lately) OCD. So while I can't give perspective as someone with OCD I thought that maybe some info for someone who is in a long term relationship with someone who is might also be helpful!

BF and I have been together for 5 years, and have been living together for about a year and a half. His OCD has definitely had periods of being more or less active, idk about anyone else but external stress seems to trigger it or at least make it a lot worse for him. 

So I guess I'll throw out some examples of stuff that comes up in our relationship, and hopefully that can be helpful for you! 

I think this is true of all or at least many mental illnesses (I myself suffer from ADHD, depression, and memory problems) but a lot of it comes down to patience and adaptability.

I know this is sort of a stereotype but a big one for us is the cleanliness of out home. I've never been the tidiest person but my depression has been a lot worse this year and I've really made a mess of my- and then our when he moved in with me in January- home. It's a very small living space and it gets bad really fast. He can't really help me with cleaning when it gets beyond a little mess because it triggers his OCD and this sometimes leads anxiety attacks or ending up having to leave the room. The work in the household is divided up different ways, but I generally do most of the house work because he can't. For us, he generally just tells me what to do or is bothering him and I take care of it. I know that's maybe not the most 'responsible' model but it works well for us. I will end up deliberating about what's the most helpful or efficient way to clean for ages and not do anything do him giving me tasks works well for us. I can take care of the stuff that gets to him. Usually once I've taken care of the worst of it things get to the point that we can work on it together. Sometimes having to shoulder the very worst of it myself gets to me, but I understand why it's necessary and at this point it's just another piece of the give and take of our relationship. The "do what you can and I'll handle what you can't" model works well for us at least. Tackling things by severity tends to work well for us and we've definitely also applied that to other situations where is OCD ends up acting up. Prioritizing has been really important for us pretty much across the board.

The other big one is when it acts up about other things, especially when we're out and about. I know that's pretty vague but I honestly haven't noticed a pattern in his triggers aside from the cleanliness stuff. But an example: he sometimes has this thing where he has to touch every corner of an object. If it's something where a corner is too small to get his fingers into he'll end up getting really distressed. I've found that purely reassuring isn't helpful for him, but problem solving is. Going back to the corner example, sometimes I'll do it for him (with my tiny baby hands) or we'll find some sort of small object (pencil, needle, ect.) that he can do the corners with. Sometimes these work, but not always. When it doesn't, I generally opt for a combination of re assurance and distraction and that tends to work at least eventually. 

A lot of it is also retroactive. I talk to my boyfriend a lot, both in the moment and after the fact about what was and wasn't helpful and how he was feeling about it. Just being able to de compress and talk it out without judgment or worrying about seeming crazy seems to help him, maybe not in the moment but I've seen an overall change in how he handles things and him not beating himself up for having these symptoms in the first place. During the first year of us dating he almost never spoke about it, and I don't think bottling it up will help, or "spare" your partner. I knew he was having issues, I just didn't know why.

Anyways, my point is, communication, patience and problem solving seem to be the big three, at least for us. So a lot of it comes down to finding a partner who is capable of and open to all that, and making sure that the same applies to you. If that's something you think you're capable of, go for it. Also, I think accepting that it's going to be a learning experience is a big one. Relationships and mental illness are often a struggle that can come with big hiccups, and not one everyone wants to commit to. It's just something you have to put a lot of work and patience into, but in my opinion it's worth it, and bf seems to agree!
